# Blur probe: where a poor photo becomes a rough read (2026-10-19)

- Pre-registered in `src/herbtwin/evals/blur_probe.py` (committed before any paid call), run from git `abe7ab6`.
- Reads: 456 (456 usable); cost $0.3588.

**Acted on:** `confidence.SURE_NAME` moves from 0.8 to 0.6, as the rule says. At 0.6 the
cost is less blur caught: 95% of heavy blur (from 100%) and 63% of medium (from 92%), with
1.3% of blurred reads named wrong and not flagged (from 0%). In all, 50 of the 300 blurred
reads lose the warning at 0.6: 7 heavy (all named right) and 43 medium (4 named wrong).

**How firm this is:** the 0.8 false-alarm interval, [0.027, 0.100], straddles the 5% bar, and
the photo read varies run to run (the soft-focus rosemary sample read "poor" on 19 Oct and
"good" here). A rerun could land on the other side of the bar.

**Post-hoc, not pre-registered (a reading, not the result):** the 9 sharp photos flagged at
0.8 are mostly hard ones: 6 dark night-flash or dim woodland shots, 3 crowded or slightly
blurred frames. 4 of the 9 were named wrong. Counted as false alarms they rule 0.8 out (6.0%);
counted as the warning doing its job, 0.8 would look better. The rule was fixed before the
data, so it decides; a larger probe with hand-labelled "is this photo really poor" could
revisit it. The judges' 6 sharp samples were all read "good" this run (the soft-focus
rosemary that read "poor" on 19 Oct read "good" at 0.9), so the guard flagged none at any
cut-off.

Rerun: `uv run --env-file .env python scripts/measure_blur_probe.py --external <main checkout>/data/external --yes-paid` (about $0.36). `--rescore` recomputes the generated block above from the committed `rows.jsonl`, for free, and keeps these notes.
